Subject: Tool calling integration patterns — post-call recap & next steps

Hi Alex + Priya — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned.

Summary from our discovery:
- Goal: add a set of domain tools (account lookup, transaction history, payments initiation) behind a single assistant UI; need predictable latency and robust error handling.
- Key constraints: PCI scope for payments (FinApps will scope card tokens to a vault), 250ms p95 routing SLA for lookup calls, and internal routing to on-prem systems for some data.
- Success metrics: 95% of user interactions resolved by the assistant without a human; end-to-end latency under 800ms for the common path.

Integration areas we discussed (where Redwood can help):
1) SDK setup & auth: recommend using our SDK for streaming + function calling. We support API key + mTLS for Dedicated/Private. For PCI, we suggest tokenized calls and a separate routing policy for payment tools.
2) Tool definitions: define each tool (name, inputs, outputs, failure modes) in a -tool-defs.json- manifest. This lets the runtime validate calls and produce structured output.
3) Routing & fallbacks: policy-based routing (region, latency, capability). We typically set a primary on-prem route with a cloud-based fallback for read-only queries.
4) Parallel tools & caching: for queries where multiple enrichers make sense (e.g., embeddings-based reranker + live DB lookup), run tools in parallel and merge with a lightweight reranker to keep latency predictable.
5) Error handling: explicit error enums in tool defs, automatic retries for idempotent ops, and deterministic fallback (e.g., show cached result + escalate to human for payments).

Attachments: I’m attaching a lightweight architecture sketch and an SDK snippet doc that shows auth examples and tool registration.

Proposed next steps:
- Technical workshop w/ your infra & FinApps eng (45–60m) — proposed times: Thu 11/26 10:00–11:00 PT or Mon 11/30 09:00–10:00 PT.
- Action: Alex/ Priya to confirm an attendee list and which systems need on-prem routing (vaults, legacy DBs).
- Redwood to provide a starter -tool-defs.json- and SDK auth snippets before the workshop.

If that all looks good I’ll drop a calendar invite and short prep doc.

Thanks,

Thanks Marissa — this is great and captures the call. A couple of clarifying Qs from the eng side before the workshop: 

1) Auth: for the on-prem vault calls we need mutual auth. You mentioned mTLS is supported — can you share a short example flow for cert rotation and how Redwood maps client certs to tenant identities?

2) Tool choice: we’re debating between letting the model directly call a payments tool (strict schema + validation) vs returning structured output that our middleware executes. Any sharp tradeoffs you’d call out?

3) Reranker: we plan to run a vector-based retriever + small cross-encoder reranker for high-precision. Is it better to run reranker inline (model calls reranker tool) or host it as a post-process in our service? Latency tradeoffs are the concern.

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finapps.com>
Cc: Priya Gupta <priya.gupta@finapps.com>, dev_patel@redwood.com, neha_kapoor@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Tool calling integration patterns — post-call recap & next steps

Alex — great questions. Quick answers below, and I’ll expand in the workshop with examples.

1) mTLS & cert rotation:
- Supported: mTLS endpoints for Dedicated/Private. Redwood’s control plane can provision short-lived client certs (7d) that map to tenant IDs. Rotation flow: Redwood issues a rotation token to your ops (via KMS/HSM integration), your provisioning service exchanges token for certs, and ops installs certs in the on-prem gateway. We also support customer-provided certs if you prefer full control.
- Mapping: cert SAN -> tenant_id claim; we log cert fingerprint + tenant mapping in the audit trail for compliance.

2) Tool calling vs structured output (middleware):
- Direct tool calling (model -> tool): pros: fewer moving parts, lower total hop latency, strong developer ergonomics. Cons: you must lock tool schemas carefully and handle partial failures in the runtime.
- Structured output (model returns an action JSON, middleware executes): pros: full control, easier to authorize/validate externally, simpler retries and idempotency handling. Cons: added hop and more infra.
- Recommendation: For payments, use middleware execution (structured output) to keep PCI scope limited to the middleware and to centralize audit/authorization. For read-only lookups where latency is critical, use direct tool calls with strict schemas + retries.

3) Reranker placement:
- If your cross-encoder is small and can meet p95 targets, inline reranking as a tool is simplest (model calls retriever -> reranker tool -> model).
- If the reranker is expensive or you need heavier batching, do it as a post-process in your service. In that case, use embeddings + a fast lightweight prefilter (approx nearest neighbors) in the model path, then call the post-process reranker async with a short blocking window and fallback to the prefilter result if it times out.

Parallel tools pattern:
- Run independent enrichers in parallel (e.g., fraud check, profile enrichment, embeddings lookup). Redwood runtime merges results and exposes a final structured payload. We add a configurable timeout for each tool and a default deterministic fallback when a tool times out.

Error handling:
- Tool defs include error enums (e.g., TIMEOUT, AUTH_FAILURE, PARTIAL_RESULT).
- Idempotency: mark side-effecting tools (payments) as non-idempotent — require explicit client acknowledgement & server-side dedupe keys.
- Retries: automatic exponential backoff for idempotent calls only.

I’ve attached a starter -tool-defs.json- with suggested fields (name, inputs, outputs, idempotent, failure_modes) and an SDK snippet that shows mTLS + API key flows.

Next step: I’ll post the workshop invite and a short prep doc with a checklist of what to bring (cert admin, example payloads, SLOs).

Thanks,
Marissa

Looping in a couple of infra notes from our side ahead of the workshop: 

- Suggested routing policy: primary -> on-prem gateway (mTLS) for read/write; fallback -> cloud-readonly endpoint with cached responses. We’ll use the request header x-redwood-route to signal routing decisions.
- Cache strategy: prefix cache for predictable queries (account lookup), TTL 5m for soft data; long-tail queries bypass cache.
- Tool timeout defaults: 250ms local, 400ms remote; overall assistant deadline 800ms. We can tune per-tool.
- Parallel tool merge: we return an ordered list of candidates with source tags, then run a micro-reranker (<=50ms budget) to pick the top result for the assistant. The micro-reranker is part of Redwood runtime and configurable per-integration.

I attached a short snippet (sdk-auth-snippets.md) with example cURL for mTLS + example Node SDK code to register a tool with a schema and failure enums.

See you on Thu — I’ll be on the call to walk through the tool-defs.json and routing policy.

— Dev
